description: We are Null Space, a Casablanca team building an AI astronaut health monitor. Combining coding (C/C++, JS, Python), AI, and sleek UI/UX, we operate like a startup to deliver a viable deep-space prototype. We welcome talents in front-end, space medicine, or pitching. Join us to build a winning solution!
summary:
Project AURA is a health-monitoring system for astronauts on long missions. Each crew member wears a watch that measures seven vital signs: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, resistive exercise, sleep and radiation dose. The watch checks every reading on board and alerts the astronaut immediately, even without contact with Earth. It then sends the data to a ground server, where mission control follows the crew on a live dashboard: colour-coded cards and graphs, a body map, the countermeasure to apply for each problem, and an archive of alerts that ground control acknowledges.

Far from Earth, messages take minutes to arrive and the link can be lost, so a crew cannot wait for a doctor's answer. AURA addresses this with on-board alerts, a local queue that keeps data safe during communication outages, and immediate countermeasures. Each vital is tied to a NASA Human Research Program risk, and the radiation thresholds are derived from NASA references. Our prototype uses simulated data and includes a solar-storm scenario.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Project AURA has three parts that work together:

1. The watch (C++ simulator). In place of the hardware, a C++ program simulates the watch worn by each astronaut. Every "mission hour" it measures seven vitals: heart rate, systolic/diastolic blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, resistive exercise minutes (against bone loss), sleep duration and daily radiation dose. It then:

- checks each reading on board against its thresholds and raises a local alert (warning or critical) at once, without waiting for Earth;

- sends the readings to the ground server over HTTP;

- keeps every reading in a local queue until the server confirms it was saved. During a simulated communication outage, readings wait on the watch and are delivered in order, with their original time, once the link returns.

It can simulate crises: a cardiovascular crisis, a fever, and a solar eruption during which the crew's radiation dose rises to critical.

2. The ground server (PHP + SQLite). It receives the readings, recomputes each status, stores everything, and turns out-of-range readings into alerts. An alert represents a problem (one astronaut, one vital) rather than one reading, so mission control isn't flooded while a value stays abnormal. Each alert keeps its first, peak and latest value, and records who acknowledged it and when.

3. The mission-control dashboard (web). It shows each astronaut's vitals as cards with a 12-hour graph in which out-of-range segments turn orange or red, a body map with status points, filters by body system, a decision log, and an alert archive with an "Acknowledge" button. Clicking a card shows the reading, the countermeasure to apply (for example "Move to the shielded area and notify mission control"), the related NASA Human Research Program risk, and where its thresholds come from. A "Live Watch Simulator" button starts the watch simulator from the dashboard, and a "Solar Flare" replay plays back a full mission day hour by hour.

BENEFITS

- Crew safety without depending on Earth: alerts and countermeasures are available on board within seconds.

- No data lost during communication outages, thanks to the watch's local queue.

- A clear, shared picture for mission control: every vital, its trend, its risk and what to do, in one screen.

- Traceability: every alert and acknowledgment is recorded.

- Continuous, passive monitoring: the astronaut doesn't have to stop working to take measurements.

INTENDED IMPACT

As missions go to the Moon and Mars, crews will be minutes away from Earth and sometimes out of contact. AURA aims to give them the autonomy NASA identifies as key for deep space: detect a health problem early, act right away, and keep mission control informed whenever the link allows. The same approach could serve people in isolated places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships or remote areas, where a doctor isn't nearby.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Watch simulator: C++17 (standard library + Winsock sockets, no external library). An equivalent PHP simulator is also included.

- Ground server: PHP 8 with SQLite (PHP built-in web server), REST API in JSON.

- Dashboard: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework. Fonts from Google Fonts.

- Data: our own simulated dataset (two astronauts, two mission days, 492 readings), built in a spreadsheet and SQL.

- Development: Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub, Windows scripts (.bat) to start everything with a double click.

- AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped write part of the code and the documentation (declared in the repository).

- Hardware: none yet. The watch is simulated; the server API is ready to receive data from a real device.

CREATIVITY

- Earth-independent by design: the watch alerts first and the ground follows, instead of the usual "send everything to the doctor and wait".

- Store-and-forward: the watch behaves like a deep-space probe, keeping data through outages and delivering it later with its original time.

- Space-specific vitals: alongside classic vitals, AURA tracks resistive exercise against bone loss, sleep and the daily radiation dose, with a solar-storm scenario.

- Grounded in NASA's own framework: each vital is linked on screen to a NASA Human Research Program risk and hazard.

- A complete chain you can try in minutes: watch, server and dashboard run on a single laptop, and a crisis can be started from a button.


FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Communication delay and outages with Earth, and the need for the crew to act alone.

- Alert fatigue: grouping repeated out-of-range readings into one alert, and showing a clear status (nominal, warning, critical) with colour and text.

- Clarity for non-experts: every alert comes with a concrete countermeasure.

- Honesty about data: all readings are simulated. Radiation thresholds are derived from NASA references (NASA-STD-3001 and Curiosity's RAD measurements); the other thresholds are illustrative and clearly marked as such.

- Ease of use and testing: no installation beyond PHP, everything runs locally, and a README guides judges step by step.

- Safety of the demo itself: the simulator can only be started from the computer running the server.

Curiosity / Mars Science Laboratory – RAD instrument (Zeitlin et al., Science, 2013)
